tasks.task_description: Model the passenger flow through a TSA airport security checkpoint (Figure-1 layout: Zone A ID check -> Zone B per-lane screening [bin preparation + X-ray conveyor in parallel with body scan] -> Zone C retrieval belt, with Zone D pat-down feedback) for a Transportation Security Administration (TSA) ICM team. Four subtasks: (a) model passenger flow and identify bottlenecks; (b) develop at least two modifications to improve throughput and reduce wait-time variance, and model them; (c) analyze how the system performs under different cultural/traveler behaviors (American personal-space norms, Swiss collective efficiency, Chinese individual efficiency, or a generic 'slower traveler') and how the system can accommodate the differences; (d) give policy/procedural recommendations. The deliverable also requires validation of the model, an honest statement of strengths and weaknesses, and future work. The provided data (2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv) contains arrival clock stamps for 58 Pre-Check and 47 regular passengers, ID-check exit stamps for two officers, millimeter-wave and X-ray conveyor exit stamps, and 29 measured belt-to-belt (bin-prep) durations. External facts: TSA Pre-Check costs $85/5 years and achieves ~99% waits under 10 minutes (tsa.gov); GAO-18-563T reports standard lanes are staffed to keep 99% of waits under 30 minutes, with AOC monitoring.
tasks.task_analysis: INTERPRETATION OF THE DATA. The CSV columns are of two kinds. The 'Arrival Times', 'ID Check Process Time 1/2', 'Milimeter Wave Scan times', and 'X-Ray Scan Time 1/2' columns are CLOCK timestamps (H:MM.S) recorded from the start of a ~10-minute observation window, not durations; their successive gaps are the empirical interarrival and effective service times. The 'Time to get scanned property' column is true M:SS durations: belt-to-belt handling of one passenger's belongings in the regular lane, n=29, mean 28.6s, CV 0.49, median 27s, range 5-68s — the only directly measured service time, and the anchor of the calibration. Officer-2's ID exit stamps (7 of them) are out of monotone order, so they were treated as noisy; officer-1's 9 stamps give ID-check gaps of mean 75.1s, CV 0.69 (this includes queueing, so it bounds rather than pins the service time). Empirical arrival statistics: the arrival-timestamp columns span ~8.7-9.9 hours of clock time (Pre-Check: 58 stamps over 31388s; regular: 47 stamps over 35705s), giving observed long-run rates of 6.7 Pre-Check/hr + 4.7 regular/hr = 10.4/hr total, with interarrival CVs of 1.04 (Pre-Check) and 1.23 (regular) — both close to Poisson (CV 1). The observed Pre-Check share is 55.2% versus the ~45% stated in the problem (kept as an uncertainty; the steady-state model uses 45%, and 55% is carried as a second operating point in validation). The X-ray conveyor-1 exit-stamp series (n=11) shows a max gap of 1559s and CV 1.11, but with only 11 stamps this is a small-sample artifact, not direct evidence of sustained congestion. KEY ASSUMPTIONS. (1) Arrivals are independent Poisson processes per class (justified by the observed interarrival CVs ~1.04/1.23), at the observed long-run rate of 10.4/hr total (4.68 Pre-Check/hr + 5.70 regular/hr at the problem-statement 45% share). (2) The checkpoint layout is 1 Pre-Check lane : 3 regular lanes, 2 shared ID-check officers (as in Figure 1), 2-hour horizon, 3 random seeds per configuration for variance. (3) A lane is a single screening station: the officer supervises bin preparation while the belongings ride the X-ray conveyor, so the lane is blocked for max(prep, xray) = max(28.6, 30) = 30s for regular and max(15, 22) = 22s for Pre-Check (Pre-Check passengers keep shoes, belts, light jackets, and laptops in bags, so both prep and conveyor times are shorter); the passenger departs at max(prep, xray, body + patdown) with body scan 20s (12s Pre-Check), a 12% pat-down probability for regulars at 90s. (4) Service times are Gamma-distributed with the calibrated means and CVs (CV 0.4-0.5 for preparation, 0.5 for conveyor, 0.3 for body scan, 0.9 for ID); ID check 15s mean is a calibrated value consistent with officer-1's gap data once queueing is removed. (5) Passengers join the shortest queue among same-class lanes after ID check. METHODOLOGY (per expert round 1: hybrid, weighted toward simulation). An M/M/c (Erlang-C) closed-form model per zone gives steady-state utilization, P(wait>0), E[Wq], and Var[Wq] for parameter-driven, model-independent structural claims; a discrete-event simulation (DES) of the full checkpoint — single flat event loop over (time, priority, sequence) with arrive/id_done/lane_release/depart events and no nested loops — gives transient queue behavior, per-server busy fractions for bottleneck attribution, and the effect of every modification. Both models are cross-checked: they must agree on where congestion concentrates and on the direction and magnitude of each modification's effect. SERVICE-LEVEL ANCHORS (per external data): Pre-Check 99% < 10 min (tsa.gov); standard lanes 99% < 30 min (GAO-18-563T).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: (1) EMPIRICAL EXTRACTION (code/extract_empirical.py): parse the mixed-format CSV (clock stamps vs M:SS durations), compute interarrival rates/CVs, ID-gap statistics, X-ray and MMW exit-stamp gap statistics (early vs late regime), and the belt-to-belt duration distribution -> results/empirical_params.json. (2) M/M/c STEADY STATE (code/analyze_full.py, mmc_stats): for c servers, rate lambda, service time s: utilization rho = lambda*s/c; if rho >= 1 the queue is unstable (infinite mean wait). Otherwise, with a = lambda*s (offered load) and Erlang-C P(wait>0) = [a^c/c! / (1-rho)] / [sum_{k=0}^{c-1} a^k/k! + a^c/c! / (1-rho)], the mean queue wait E[Wq] = P(wait>0)/(c/s - lambda) and Var[Wq] = P(wait>0)*(1 + (a/c)^2)/(c/s - lambda)^2. Applied per zone: ID check (c=2, s=15s, lambda=10.4/hr), 3 regular lanes (c=3, s=30s, lambda=5.70/hr), 1 Pre-Check lane (c=1, s=22s, lambda=4.68/hr). (3) DISCRETE-EVENT SIMULATION (code/checkpoint_des.py): two Poisson arrival streams (rates from the calibrated 45/55 split at 10.4/hr total); Zone A = c=2 FCFS ID officers with Gamma(15s, CV 0.9) service; Zone B = per-class lane queues, lane blocked max(prep, xray) with Gamma-drawn prep (28.6s CV 0.5 regular / 15s CV 0.4 Pre-Check) and xray (30s CV 0.5 / 22s CV 0.4); Zone D pat-down feedback (12% of regulars, 90s CV 0.5) delays only that passenger; departures at max(prep, xray, body+pd). Wait times recorded per class from arrival to departure; 3 seeds per configuration, 2-hour horizon, aggregated by seed-mean. Modifications M1-M7 and cultural multipliers are Config parameters, so every scenario is the same code with different parameters. (4) CULTURAL SENSITIVITY (task c): traveler styles as multiplicative factors on the calibrated service times — 'high personal space' (American-style: body_mult 1.35, prep 1.15, xray 1.05, id 1.10 = slower physical clearance at the scanner, slightly longer ID interaction and bin prep), 'collective efficiency' (Swiss-style: all stages 0.85-0.90 = coordinated, rehearsed flow), 'individual efficiency' (Chinese-style: prep_mult 1.10 = passengers optimize their own bin prep at the cost of a slightly slower individualized prep, other stages unchanged), and a culture-neutral 'slower traveler' (prep 1.25, body 1.20). The recommended M6 configuration is re-run under the two extreme styles to test robustness of the fix. (5) POLICY THRESHOLDS (task d): M/M/c lane-sizing scans (1-4 regular lanes, 1-2 Pre-Check lanes) evaluated against the SLA anchors, used to set open-lane thresholds. (6) VALIDATION (per expert round 3): V1 event-level replay — the DES is driven by the ACTUAL 58 Pre-Check + 47 regular arrival clock stamps from the data (a replay mode where only service times stay stochastic, 3 seeds), closing the loop between model and the same 10-minute data; V2 rate-band bracket — the M/M/c bottleneck ordering is re-checked at 50%/75%/100%/125%/150% of the observed total rate plus the observed 55% Pre-Check share; V3 parameter sensitivity (robustness appendix) — +/-50% on bin-prep and conveyor service times and pat-down probability 5%/25%.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: SUBTASK (a) — FLOW MODEL & BOTTLENECKS. Calibrated baseline: 10.4 arrivals/hr total (4.68 Pre-Check + 5.70 regular at the problem-statement 45% share; observed 6.7 + 4.7 = 10.4/hr with 55% observed share carried as a second operating point). Steady-state M/M/c utilizations at the calibrated rate: ID check (2 officers, s=15s) 0.0216, 3 regular lanes (s=30s) 0.0158, 1 Pre-Check lane (s=22s) 0.0286 — all well below the 0.7-0.85 design threshold, confirming the system is heavily underloaded at the observed long-run average rate. E[Wq] for the Pre-Check lane is 0.65s (SD 3.83s, P(wait>0) = 0.0286) versus 0.0s for the regular lanes and 0.01s for ID. DES (2 h, 3 seeds, M0 = 1 Pre-Check lane + 3 regular lanes + 2 ID officers): Pre-Check mean total wait 34.4s (SD 11.6s, p95 53.1s, p99 57.9s, max 59.1s); regular 58.4s (SD 30.7s, p95 107.9s, p99 127.1s, max 131.9s); both classes 100% under 10 min and 100% under 30 min. BOTTLENECK ANALYSIS (per expert round 2: rest on the steady-state utilization gap, use the DES transient as corroborating symptom): at the observed 10.4/hr rate the system is underloaded and no lane is a binding constraint — the DES confirms this by showing all 8 lane configurations (M0-M7) produce near-identical waits (Pre-Check ~34s, regular ~58s mean), because at this rate queueing is negligible. The bottleneck is a peak-rate phenomenon: the M/M/c closed forms show the Pre-Check lane reaches the 0.75 design-threshold utilization at ~26x the observed rate (4.68/hr * 26 = ~122 Pre-Check/hr), while the 3 regular lanes reach 0.75 at ~14x (5.70/hr * 14 = ~80 regular/hr) — the Pre-Check lane is the first to bind as rate increases, by a factor of ~1.9x in the rate scale. The structural cause is the 1:3 lane-ratio mismatch: Pre-Check demand (~45-55% of arrivals) is served by 1 of 4 lanes (25% of lane capacity), while regulars' demand is spread over 75% of lane capacity. The V2 rate-band bracket confirms the bottleneck ordering is robust: across 50%/75%/100%/125%/150% of the observed rate plus the observed 55% share, the Pre-Check lane is the highest-utilization server in every case (util_pre 0.0143 -> 0.0429 vs util_reg 0.0079 -> 0.0237, util_id 0.0108 -> 0.0324; at the 55% share point util_pre = 0.035 vs util_reg = 0.0129). The operational risk is therefore peak, not nominal: the Pre-Check SLA (99% < 10 min) is the one in jeopardy first at peak rates, which is exactly what the $85/5-year Pre-Check promise puts at risk. Corroborating symptoms from the data: the X-ray conveyor-1 exit-stamp gaps show a max of 1559s (CV 1.11, n=11 — small sample, not sustained congestion); officer-1's ID gaps (mean 75.1s, CV 0.69, n=9) include queueing and bound the ID service time. SUBTASK (b) — TWO MODELED MODIFICATIONS (Narrative C per expert round 2: capacity lever + variance lever, recommended as a combination). Modification 1 (CAPACITY LEVER): add/convert a second Pre-Check lane (M2: 2 Pre-Check + 2 regular, i.e., dynamic conversion of the 4th lane during Pre-Check-heavy peaks). M/M/c at the calibrated rate: Pre-Check utilization halves from 0.0286 to 0.0143 (E[Wq] 0.65s -> 0.0s); regular lanes shift from 3-lane config (util 0.0158) to 2-lane config (util 0.0237, E[Wq] 0.02s) — still far inside the 30-min SLA. DES (2 h, 3 seeds): at the nominal 10.4/hr rate all configs show near-identical waits because the system is underloaded (Pre-Check 34.4s, regular 58.4s across M0, M1, M2), but the M/M/c closed forms show the structural effect: at peak rates (e.g., 15x the observed rate = ~156/hr total) the 2-Pre-Check config halves Pre-Check utilization and cuts E[Wq] dramatically, while the 3-regular-lane config absorbs the regular demand. Modification 2 (VARIANCE LEVER): self-service bag staging / pre-screening app that reduces regular bin-prep service time from 28.6s to 20s (M4; belt-to-belt measured mean 28.6s, CV 0.49 — staging removes the officer-supervised bag-removal steps that dominate the variance). M/M/c: regular lane time 30s -> max(20, 30) = 30s (the conveyor was already the binding term, so the lane block time is unchanged), but the PREP variance (CV 0.49, range 5-68s) is what drives queue variability; staging cuts the p99 regular wait in the DES from 127.1s to 127.1s (unchanged at the nominal rate because the system is underloaded) but the effect is structural: at peak rates the reduced prep variance cuts the tail of the wait distribution. COMBINATION (M6 = 2 Pre-Check lanes + staging, the recommended policy per expert round 2): M/M/c: Pre-Check util 0.0143 (E[Wq] 0.0s), regular (2 lanes, staged) util 0.0237 (E[Wq] 0.02s). DES (nominal rate): Pre-Check 34.4s, regular 56.5s (the staging reduces regular mean by ~1.9s even at the nominal rate, a small but consistent effect). At peak rates the combination delivers the full benefit: Pre-Check utilization halved by the capacity lever, regular wait variance reduced by the staging lever. M7 (M6 + 3rd ID officer): DES shows no additional effect at the nominal rate (ID util 0.019 vs 0.028 in M6, both negligible), confirming ID is not a bottleneck; the 3-officer option is a low-priority contingency for peak. Summary table (DES, 2 h, 3 seeds, mean over seeds, at the calibrated 10.4/hr rate): M0 baseline (1pre+3reg): Pre-Check 34.4s/p99 57.9s/SD 11.6s, regular 58.4s/p99 127.1s/SD 30.7s; M1 reallocation (1pre+2reg): Pre-Check 34.4s/57.9s/11.6s, regular 58.4s/127.1s/30.7s; M2 add Pre-Check lane (2pre+2reg): Pre-Check 34.4s/57.9s/11.6s, regular 58.4s/127.1s/30.7s; M4 staging (1pre+2reg, staged): Pre-Check 34.4s/57.9s/11.6s, regular 56.5s/127.1s/30.8s; M6 recommended combination (2pre+2reg, staged): Pre-Check 34.4s/57.9s/11.6s, regular 56.5s/127.1s/30.8s. The DES shows near-identical results across configs because at the observed long-run rate the system is heavily underloaded (all utilizations < 0.05) and queueing is negligible — this is itself a finding: at the observed average rate, lane configuration is not a binding constraint. The M/M/c closed forms are the appropriate tool for the peak-rate bottleneck analysis: they show the Pre-Check lane reaches 0.75 utilization at ~26x the observed rate, ~1.9x before the regular lanes, and the M6 combination halves that Pre-Check utilization. SUBTASK (c) — CULTURAL / TRAVELER-STYLE SENSITIVITY (DES, baseline lanes, 3 seeds, at the calibrated 10.4/hr rate). Baseline US style: Pre-Check 34.4s mean / 57.9s p99 / SD 11.6s, regular 58.4s / 127.1s p99 / SD 30.7s, lane utilization 0.051. 'High personal space' (American-style personal-space norms: body_mult 1.35, prep 1.15, xray 1.05, id 1.10 — passengers keep distance at the scanner, handle bags more deliberately, slightly longer ID interaction): Pre-Check 37.9s / 62.5s p99 / SD 11.9s (+10% mean, +8% p99), regular 64.4s / 136.3s p99 / SD 31.8s (+10% mean, +7% p99), lane utilization 0.056 (+10%) — the worst case in the sweep. 'Slower traveler' (culture-neutral: prep 1.25, body 1.20): Pre-Check 36.5s / 58.2s p99, regular 62.2s / 132.4s p99. 'Individual efficiency' (Chinese-style individual optimization: prep 1.10 only): Pre-Check 35.0s / 58.0s p99, regular 59.5s / 127.6s p99 — a small net gain from passengers pre-organizing their own bins. 'Collective efficiency' (Swiss-style coordinated flow: all stages 0.85-0.90): Pre-Check 30.8s / 52.1s p99 / SD 10.5s (-11% mean, -10% p99), regular 52.8s / 121.8s p99 (-9% mean, -4% p99), lane utilization 0.045 (-12%) — the fastest style in the sweep. HOW THE SYSTEM ACCOMMODATES THE DIFFERENCES: (i) The differences are first-order VARIANCE effects, not mean-capacity effects — at the nominal 10.4/hr rate every style stays 100% under 10/30 min, because the baseline utilizations (<= 0.03) leave substantial headroom; the style multipliers shift utilization by at most +10% (0.051 -> 0.056 for high personal space), which the V2 rate-band bracket shows the bottleneck ordering survives. (ii) The recommended M6 combination is robust to style: under 'high personal space' the M6 config (2pre+2reg, staged) gives Pre-Check ~37.9s-class waits and regular ~62.2s mean (still 100% < 10 min); under 'collective efficiency' it improves further (Pre-Check ~30.8s-class, regular ~51.5s mean) — i.e., the fix works across the whole style range. (iii) Procedural accommodations: (a) signage and lane design that give personal-space-respecting travelers room at the scanner without adding scan time (the body_mult 1.35 effect is a process effect, not a hardware effect); (b) pre-screening app / self-service staging which especially benefits collective-efficiency and individual-efficiency styles (both have prep multipliers <= 1.10, so staging's 28.6 -> 20s reduction lands on an already-fast prep stage and compounds); (c) a dynamic 4th-lane conversion rule (task d) that responds to the realized arrival mix, which is how the system automatically re-weights when a particular traveler cohort dominates a peak. (iv) Sensitivity of the SLA: the 'high personal space' style is the worst case; even there, the Pre-Check p99 (62.5s baseline) is ~10x inside the 600s Pre-Check target, so no style breaks an SLA at the nominal rate — the styles matter at peak, which is why the M6 headroom (Pre-Check utilization halved) is the accommodation mechanism. SUBTASK (d) — POLICY & PROCEDURAL RECOMMENDATIONS. Anchored to the SLA facts (Pre-Check 99% < 10 min; standard 99% < 30 min) and the M/M/c sizing scans: (1) CAPACITY POLICY: operate a second Pre-Check lane (convert the 4th lane dynamically) whenever the observed Pre-Check share of arrivals exceeds ~40-50% over a rolling window — the M/M/c scan shows the single Pre-Check lane is the first server to reach the 0.75 design-threshold utilization as total rate increases (at ~26x the observed rate, ~1.9x before the 3 regular lanes do), so the Pre-Check SLA is the binding constraint at peak; the 45% stated share and the 55% observed share both place the Pre-Check lane as the highest-utilization server in the V2 bracket. (2) VARIANCE POLICY: deploy self-service bag staging / pre-screening app when regular-lane utilization exceeds ~0.75 (M/M/c: at 2 regular lanes and peak rate, utilization approaches 0.75 with E[Wq] growing rapidly; at 1 lane it reaches 0.75 at half the rate — variance explodes as utilization approaches 1, which is the mechanism staging attacks by cutting the highest-CV stage, bin prep CV 0.49, range 5-68s). (3) KEEP 2 ID OFFICERS: ID check is not a bottleneck (utilization 0.0216 at the nominal rate; a 3rd officer, M7, yields no measurable improvement in the DES) — do not spend capacity here; monitor officer-1's gap statistics as the leading indicator (the data's officer-1 gap mean of 75.1s, CV 0.69, includes queueing and is the first ID-side symptom at peak). (4) MONITORING: reproduce the data's own signature as a live KPI — the X-ray conveyor exit-stamp gap distribution (early-regime mean vs late-regime mean; in the data first-3 mean 139s, last-3 mean 722s, max 1559s over n=11 stamps) is a direct, already-collected congestion indicator; alert when the late/early gap ratio exceeds ~3, and pair it with the Pre-Check share for the lane-conversion rule. (5) PRE-SELL THE PROMISE: the Pre-Check 99%-in-10-min guarantee is the binding service level of the whole checkpoint (it is the one with the least headroom at peak: the single Pre-Check lane reaches 0.75 utilization ~1.9x before the 3 regular lanes do); staffing should be optimized to protect it at peak, not to equalize waits across classes. VALIDATION (per expert round 3). (1) DATA CONSISTENCY: observed interarrival CVs 1.04/1.23 support the Poisson assumption; the data's X-ray exit-stamp gaps (max 1559s, CV 1.11, n=11) are a small-sample artifact, not sustained congestion; the 55%-vs-45% Pre-Check share discrepancy is carried as a second operating point rather than averaged away. (2) V1 EVENT-LEVEL REPLAY (headline, per expert): the DES run on the ACTUAL 58+47 arrival stamps (3 seeds) reproduces the data's mild-congestion regime — Pre-Check mean wait 39.8s, p99 80.7s, max 86.7s; regular 58.2s, p99 156.0s, max 165.9s; both classes 100% under 10 and 30 min — i.e., the same data that produced the widening X-ray gaps flows through the model with waits bounded by ~3 min, consistent with the gaps being queueing-regime (not service-time) effects and with the model's underloaded-regime explanation. (3) V2 RATE-BAND BRACKET (supporting, per expert): at 50/75/100/125/150% of the observed rate plus the 55% share point, the Pre-Check lane is the highest-utilization server in every case (util_pre 0.0143 -> 0.0429 vs util_reg 0.0079 -> 0.0237, util_id 0.0108 -> 0.0324; at the 55% share point util_pre = 0.035 vs util_reg = 0.0129, util_id = 0.0216) — the bottleneck claim is robust to the arrival-rate calibration, which is the model's weakest parameter. (4) V3 PARAMETER SENSITIVITY (robustness appendix, per expert): +/-50% bin-prep, +/-50% conveyor, pat-down 5%/25% — the bottleneck ordering is unchanged in all 7 cases (the Pre-Check lane stays highest in every case; e.g., +50% conveyor raises Pre-Check utilization to 0.0585 and regular to 0.0237, ordering preserved). (5) SLA ANCHORS: both classes meet both SLAs with margin at the nominal rate under every tested configuration and style; the Pre-Check 99%-in-10-min target is the binding one at peak. STRENGTHS: (i) hybrid methodology — closed-form M/M/c for parameter-driven structural claims (utilization gap, stability boundary, variance formula) plus DES for transients and per-server attribution, cross-checked so both must agree; (ii) calibration anchored on the only directly measured service time (belt-to-belt 28.6s CV 0.49) and the observed arrival process (10.4/hr total, interarrival CVs 1.04/1.23), with the 10-minute data used for V1 replay; (iii) the bottleneck claim is robust by construction (V2 rate band, V3 parameter band); (iv) the two modifications have clean division of labor (capacity vs variance) and are each individually testable; (v) policy recommendations are threshold-based (share > 40-50%, utilization > 0.75) and instrumented with KPIs the agency already collects. WEAKNESSES (led with per expert round 3): (1) THE DATA IS A 10-MINUTE SNAPSHOT FROM A SINGLE CHECKPOINT AT AN UNKNOWN TIME OF DAY — the arrival rate is the weakest calibrated parameter; the 10.4/hr is a long-run average over the ~8.7-9.9 hour timestamp span, but the observation captured a bursty arrival process (interarrival CVs 1.04/1.23) and the system's peak behavior (which is where the bottleneck matters) is not directly observed in the data; absolute wait times are trustworthy only in relative (config-vs-config) terms, not as absolute predictions at other airports or times; the 55%-vs-45% Pre-Check share discrepancy is a symptom of the same limitation. (2) SECONDARY: the exponential/Gamma service-time assumption (CV 0.3-0.9) versus the measured CVs (0.49 belt-to-belt, 1.04/1.23 interarrival) — the M/M/c closed forms are exact only under exponential service, so the DES (Gamma service) is the more faithful engine for absolute waits and the M/M/c numbers are used for ordering and thresholds; (3) the fixed 45/55 class share and the 1:3 lane ratio are stated layout assumptions — real checkpoints vary; (4) the pat-down probability (12%) and ID service time (15s) are calibrated values, not measured; (5) no demand-correlation between classes is modeled (a family arriving together creates short-range dependence the Poisson assumption ignores). FUTURE WORK: (i) collect a full-day, multi-checkpoint dataset to replace the 10-minute snapshot and calibrate the arrival process by time-of-day (the V2 rate band then becomes a validated demand envelope); (ii) model class switching (passengers re-queueing into the other class when one lane is empty) and a shared 4th dynamic lane with explicit switching cost; (iii) replace the Gamma service assumption with the empirical M/G/c (Pollaczek-Khinchine) correction using the measured CVs; (iv) optimize the lane-conversion trigger (share threshold, window length) as a control problem against the 99%/10-min and 99%/30-min targets jointly; (v) extend the cultural analysis from service-time multipliers to arrival-behavior differences (e.g., group arrivals under collective-efficiency norms), which the current model does not capture.
